facts.text: The great cormorant's plumage is largely black, with bronze to greenish shine on the wings and tail and a purple tinge on the body.
facts.quote: The plumage is largely black, but with bronze to greenish iridescence on the wings and tail, and purple iridescence on the body.

facts.text: Adult great cormorants have striking deep sea-green eyes, while juveniles have duller dark grey ones.
facts.quote: The eyes are a striking deep sea-green in adults, duller dark grey in juveniles.

facts.text: The great cormorant is mostly silent but makes various guttural noises at its breeding colonies.
facts.quote: Great cormorants are mostly silent, but they make various guttural noises at their breeding colonies.

facts.text: Great cormorant pairs reuse the same nest site to breed year after year.
facts.quote: Pairs will use the same nest site to breed year after year.

facts.text: The great cormorant lays three to five pale blue or green eggs, which are sometimes covered in a white chalky layer.
facts.quote: They lay a clutch of three to five eggs that measure 63 by 41 millimetres (2+1⁄2 by 1+5⁄8 in) on average. The eggs are a pale blue or green, and sometimes have a white chalky layer covering them.

facts.text: The great cormorant catches fish by diving, with dives lasting one to three minutes and reaching depths of up to 9.5 metres.
facts.quote: The duration of its dives varies from 1–3 minutes, with the bird diving to depths of up to a maximum of 9.5 metres (31 ft).

facts.text: In summer great cormorants eat any fish of suitable size they can catch, but in winter they prefer larger, torpedo-shaped fish.
facts.quote: Cormorants consume all fish of appropriate size that they are able to catch in summer and noticeably select for larger, mostly torpedo-shaped fish in winter.

facts.text: Great cormorants can hear well underwater, which may help them detect fish, though this comes at the cost of reduced hearing sensitivity in air.
facts.quote: Studies suggest that their hearing has evolved for underwater usage, possibly aiding their detection of fish. These adaptations also have a cost on their hearing ability in air which is of lowered sensitivity.

facts.text: In China and Japan, fishermen traditionally use great cormorants to catch fish, tying a line around their throats so the birds cannot swallow the larger fish.
facts.quote: In this practice, fishermen tie a line around the throats of cormorants, tight enough to prevent swallowing the larger fish they catch, and deploy them from small boats.

facts.text: In northern Norway, gathering cormorants are seen as good luck, and the birds are traditionally regarded as semi-sacred.
facts.quote: In North Norway, cormorants are traditionally seen as semi-sacred. It is regarded as good luck to have cormorants gather near your village or settlement.
